item.title: WordPress wp2shell RCE, OpenSSL HollowByte, ViteVenom npm RAT, and Abbott Probe
item.content:encoded:
New wp2shell WordPress Core Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code — Must Read

WordPress patched a critical core flaw dubbed wp2shell that allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on default 6.9 and 7.0 installations via the REST API batch endpoint. Site owners should verify they are running 6.9.5 or 7.0.2, because there is no CVE yet and scanners may not detect vulnerable versions.

  • WordPress released versions 6.9.5 and 7.0.2 on July 17, 2026 to fix a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw in core that could be triggered by an anonymous request against a default install with no plugins.
  • The affected WordPress versions are 6.9.0 through 6.9.4, fixed in 6.9.5, and 7.0.0 through 7.0.1, fixed in 7.0.2.
  • Adam Kues at Assetnote, Searchlight Cyber’s attack surface management arm, reported the flaw through WordPress’s HackerOne program, and Searchlight published a writeup under the name wp2shell while withholding technical details.
  • WordPress described the issue as a REST API batch-route confusion and SQL injection issue leading to remote code execution, but neither advisory had a CVE ID or CVSS score by July 18.
  • Searchlight’s temporary mitigation advice is to block anonymous access to the batch endpoint by blocking both /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1, disabling unauthenticated REST API access, or using a drop-in plugin until the site is updated.

Unauthenticated RCE in WordPress core (wp2shell) — Must Read

WordPress released emergency updates for an unauthenticated RCE in core affecting versions 6.9.0–6.9.4 and 7.0.0–7.0.1, with fixes in 6.9.5 and 7.0.2. Site owners should patch immediately or temporarily block the vulnerable REST batch endpoint until updated.

  • WordPress released emergency security update 7.0.2 on July 17 to fix an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in WordPress core that can affect stock installs with no plugins involved.
  • The flaw is described as a REST API batch-route confusion and SQL injection issue that chains into remote code execution through the `/wp-json/batch/v1` endpoint.
  • The remote code execution flaw affects WordPress 6.9.0 through 6.9.4, WordPress 7.0.0 through 7.0.1, and WordPress 7.1 beta, with fixes in 6.9.5, 7.0.2, and 7.1 beta2.
  • WordPress.org has turned on forced auto-updates for affected sites, but the article says site owners should still confirm their version in the dashboard.
  • If immediate updating is not possible, the article lists temporary mitigations such as blocking unauthenticated REST API access, blocking `/wp-json/batch/v1` and `rest_route=/batch/v1`, or requiring authentication on the REST batch route.

Abbott Laboratories probes two cyber incidents amid extortion claims — Should Read

Abbott Laboratories is investigating two cyber incidents: confirmed unauthorized access to legacy Exact Sciences systems in its Cancer Diagnostics business claimed by ShinyHunters, and a separate alleged LabCentral portal breach. Abbott says operations, product availability, and patient services are unaffected, while the attackers claim they stole large amounts of sensitive data that has not been independently verified.

  • Abbott Laboratories is investigating unauthorized access to a limited number of internal legacy Exact Sciences systems in its Cancer Diagnostics business.
  • Abbott said the Cancer Diagnostics incident does not affect business operations, product availability, manufacturing or lab operations, its ability to serve patients, or other Abbott businesses and systems.
  • ShinyHunters claimed it accessed Abbott through a mid-June vishing attack that compromised a Microsoft Entra single sign-on account and allowed access to internal systems.
  • ShinyHunters claimed it stole data from Microsoft Entra, ServiceNow, SharePoint, Databricks, and Coupa, including internal documents, contracts, customer information, and large datasets containing personal and medical-related information, but BleepingComputer has not independently verified those claims.
  • Abbott is also investigating a separate potential incident involving its LabCentral customer portal, but said the portal contains publicly available technical product reference documents and does not contain proprietary, sensitive customer, or business information.

Seven Malicious Vite npm Packages Use Blockchain C2 to Deliver a RAT — Should Read

Researchers found seven malicious npm packages impersonating Vite ecosystem tooling that use blockchain-based command-and-control infrastructure to fetch and run a RAT. Developers who installed them should remove the packages, audit dependencies, rotate credentials, and check shell profile files for persistence changes.

  • Checkmarx researchers discovered seven malicious npm packages targeting developers using the Vite JavaScript and frontend build tool ecosystem.
  • The campaign, called ViteVenom, is linked to the threat actor SuccessKey and is described as an expansion of the earlier ChainVeil campaign.
  • The malicious packages use blockchain-based command-and-control infrastructure involving Tron, Aptos, and Binance Smart Chain to retrieve payloads and deliver a remote access trojan.
  • Unlike ChainVeil’s unscoped typosquats, ViteVenom uses scoped package names that impersonate the @vitejs/* namespace to appear more legitimate.
  • Users who installed the packages are advised to remove them immediately, audit dependencies, rotate credentials, and check .bashrc, .zshrc, and .profile files for unauthorized changes.

OpenSSL HollowByte Flaw Could Freeze Server Memory with 11-Byte TLS Requests — Should Read

OpenSSL quietly fixed a denial-of-service flaw dubbed HollowByte that lets an attacker trigger persistent server memory growth with tiny malformed TLS handshake requests, potentially exhausting memory on glibc-based systems. Because the fix received no CVE or advisory, organizations may need to verify manually that they have upgraded or backported the June 9 OpenSSL patches.

  • Okta's Red Team reported an OpenSSL denial-of-service flaw named HollowByte that can make an unpatched server allocate up to 131 KB of memory from an 11-byte TLS request for a message body that never arrives.
  • OpenSSL fixed HollowByte in releases 4.0.1, 3.6.3, 3.5.7, 3.4.6, and 3.0.21 dated June 9, but assigned no CVE, advisory, or changelog entry to the fix.
  • The flaw occurs because older OpenSSL versions grew the TLS receive buffer to the peer-declared handshake message length as soon as the header arrived, before the body appeared and before handshake checks ran.
  • In Okta's tests on glibc systems, freed buffers were not returned to the kernel, heap fragmentation caused resident memory to remain elevated, and an NGINX server with 1 GB of memory was OOM-killed with 547 MB frozen in fragments.
  • The fix covers TLS only, while the article says the DTLS handshake path still sizes its buffer from the length declared by the peer and has not been classified or committed for fixing by OpenSSL.

June Incident Response Insights — Optional

Booz Allen is promoting its June Incident Response Insights Report, which summarizes intelligence from more than 1,000 real-world incident response engagements to help organizations understand current threat actor activity and improve resilience.

  • The article announces the June Incident Response Insights Report dated July 17, 2026.
  • Booz Allen’s Incident Response Insights Report is based on intelligence from more than 1,000 real-world engagements annually.
  • The report aims to show what threat actors are doing, where the threat landscape is headed, and what Booz Allen has encountered on the frontlines this month.
  • The report is presented by Booz Allen, identified as a Health-ISAC Community Services Champion.
